children.text: Use ideal gases with five molecular degrees of freedom for air, so molar cp=7R/2. Constants: solar irradiance Fs=1370 W/m², albedo a=0.30, σ=\(5.67\times10^{-8}\) W m⁻² K⁻⁴, molar masses μw=0.018 kg/mol and μair=0.029 kg/mol, R=8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Earth radiates as a blackbody. In the one-layer model use shortwave transmission tsw and longwave transmission tlw, with the remaining absorbed power re-radiated equally upwards and downwards as prescribed by the exercise. All atmospheric parcels stay in pressure equilibrium with their surroundings. Gravity g is uniform and downward. Define lapse rate Γ=−dT/dz, positive when air cools with height. Latent heat L is per mass and may be treated constant over the temperature interval. In E use air index one and ice index n=1.31.

statement.text:
Atmospheric physics
Use ideal gases with five molecular degrees of freedom for air, so molar cp=7R/2. Constants: solar irradiance Fs=1370 W/m², albedo a=0.30, σ=\(5.67\times10^{-8}\) W m⁻² K⁻⁴, molar masses μw=0.018 kg/mol and μair=0.029 kg/mol, R=8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Earth radiates as a blackbody. In the one-layer model use shortwave transmission tsw and longwave transmission tlw, with the remaining absorbed power re-radiated equally upwards and downwards as prescribed by the exercise. All atmospheric parcels stay in pressure equilibrium with their surroundings. Gravity g is uniform and downward. Define lapse rate Γ=−dT/dz, positive when air cools with height. Latent heat L is per mass and may be treated constant over the temperature interval. In E use air index one and ice index n=1.31.

a.1. Absorbed solar power
Find total net solar power P0 received by Earth plus atmosphere using Earth radius RE.
a.2. Airless temperature
Ignoring the atmosphere find steady ground temperature Tg0.
a.3. One-layer greenhouse temperature
For tsw=0.9 and tlw=0.2 calculate Tg.
b.1. Diatomic vibrational frequency
Two atoms mA,mB are connected by a spring of stiffness k. Find their vibrational angular frequency.
b.2. Vibrational photon
Find photon energy for a transition between adjacent vibrational levels, neglecting recoil.
b.3. Doppler-shift convention
A molecule moves with speed v>0 towards the emitter. Find the first-order line shift. Distinguish the frequency it sees for fixed incident lab light from the lab frequency resonant with its transition f0.
b.4. Velocity normalization
Normalize p1(v)=Cexp[−mv²/(2kBT)] over the real line.
b.5. Thermal spectral profile
Find p2(f), up to normalization, for a rest line f0 broadened by one-dimensional thermal motion.
b.6. Doppler width and sketch
Sketch p2 against f−f0 and find f*−f0 at 1/e of the peak.
c.1. Hydrostatic pressure gradient

Derive dp/dz using density ρ and g.
c.2. Ideal-gas gradient
Express dp/dz through μair,g,p,T and R.
c.3. Isothermal barometric law
For constant T and surface pressure p0 find p(z).
c.4. Dry adiabatic lapse rate
Find Γa for a rising adiabatic parcel using molar cp.
c.5. Buoyancy stability
An initially equilibrated parcel is displaced by δz in atmosphere of lapse Γ. Derive its linear equation, stability condition and angular frequency.
d.1. Clausius-Clapeyron slope
Find dps/dT for liquid-vapour coexistence using L,μw,ps,T and R. Neglect liquid volume relative to vapour.
d.2. Saturation-pressure law
At T0 let ps=ps0. Find ps(T) assuming constant L.
d.3. Cloud formation temperature
A moist parcel starts at Ti=17.0°C,pi=\(10^{5}\) Pa with fixed water mass fraction φ=0.010. Find Tl where condensation begins. Use L=\(2.460\times10^{6}\) J/kg and ps0=1940 Pa at Ti. Treat cp=7R/2 and use the dilute-water approximation.
e.1. Prism deviation law

For prism apex angle φ, refractive index n and incident angle α from the face normal, derive outgoing deviation δ.
e.2. Hexagonal-ice deviation plot

The ray traverses the two rectangular faces indicated in the source hexagon, equivalent to φ=60°. For n=1.31 tabulate and plot δ from α=20° to 70° in 5° increments.
e.3. Bright halo angle
At what angular distance from the Sun is the halo brightest?

children.text: Use the intercepting disc and the absorbed fraction: \(P_0=(1-a)\pi R_E^2F_s\).
Equate absorbed disc power to emission over 4πRE²: \(T_{g0}=[(1-a)F_s/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}\simeq255\,\mathrm K\), about −18°C.

Let PE be ground emission and PA the emission of each atmospheric face. Surface balance gives PE=PA+tswP0. Top-of-atmosphere balance gives tlwPE+PA=P0. Hence \(T_g=[(1+t_{sw})/(1+t_{lw})]^{1/4}T_{g0}\simeq286\,\mathrm K\), about 13°C.
The relative coordinate has reduced mass μ=mAmB/(mA+mB). Thus \(\omega_d=\sqrt{k(m_A+m_B)/(m_Am_B)}\).

For fixed incoming lab frequency fin, the molecule sees f′≈fin(1+v/c). Thus if fin=f0 the observed shift is +f0v/c, the convention used in the official solution. If f0 instead denotes the molecule's rest-frame absorption resonance, the resonant laboratory incident frequency is \(f=f_0/(1+v/c)\simeq f_0-f_0v/c\), with shift −f0v/c. The source wording mixes these descriptions. Both yield the same symmetric thermal line profile below, so this signed convention item uses self-review.
The Gaussian integral is √(2πkBT/m), so \(C=\sqrt{m/(2\pi k_BT)}\).
Use |v|=c|f−f0|/f0 and the constant Jacobian c/f0. Thus \[p_2(f)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{mc^2(f-f_0)^2}{2k_BT f_0^2}\right].\] If normalized, the prefactor is (c/f0)√[m/(2πkBT)].
The curve is a symmetric Gaussian centred at zero, decaying to zero in both tails. The 1/e points are \(f_*-f_0=\pm f_0\sqrt{2k_BT/(mc^2)}\). The field checks the positive half-width.
Balance upward minus downward pressure forces on area A and height dz against weight ρgA dz. This gives \(dp/dz=-\rho g\).
Adiabatic enthalpy change balances gravitational potential: cp dT+μairg dz=0. Equivalently combine pVγ=constant with hydrostatic equilibrium. Thus \(\Gamma_a=\mu_{air}g/c_p\).

Parcel and environment temperatures become T−Γaδz and T−Γδz. At equal pressure ρ∝1/T, so net buoyancy acceleration is \[\delta\ddot z=\frac gT(\Gamma-\Gamma_a)\delta z.\] Stability requires Γ<Γa, with \(\omega=\sqrt{g(\mu_{air}g/c_p-\Gamma)/T}\). Equality is neutral, while Γ>Γa gives exponential growth. This sign follows the defined positive lapse rate.
For evaporated mass m, ΔS=Lm/T while ΔV≈(m/μw)RT/ps. Thus \(d p_s/dT=\mu_w Lp_s/(RT^2)\).

The water partial pressure is \(p_w\simeq\phi(\mu_{air}/\mu_w)p\), and dry adiabatic ascent gives p=pi(T/Ti)cp/R. Solve \[\phi\frac{\mu_{air}}{\mu_w}p_i(T_l/T_i)^{7/2}=p_{s0}\exp\left[-\frac{\mu_wL}{R}(1/T_l-1/T_i)\right]\] for the first lower-temperature crossing. With Ti=290.15 K the root is Tl≈286.8 K, or 13.7°C. The total-mass definition of φ changes this only slightly beyond the dilute approximation.

Snell gives internal entry α′=arcsin(sinα/n) and internal exit β′=φ−α′. The external exit angle is β=arcsin(nsinβ′). Therefore \[\delta=\alpha+\arcsin\{n\sin[\varphi-\arcsin(\sin\alpha/n)]\}-\varphi.\] A transmitted ray requires the exit sine magnitude no greater than one.

The (α,δ) pairs in degrees are approximately (20,27.5),(25,24.6),(30,23.0),(35,22.2),(40,21.8),(45,22.0),(50,22.5),(55,23.4),(60,24.7),(65,26.5),(70,28.7). Draw a smooth curve with a minimum close to α=41°. Label both axes in degrees.

The random crystal orientations concentrate rays near minimum deviation. Symmetric passage gives \(\delta_{min}=2\arcsin[n\sin(\varphi/2)]-\varphi\simeq21.8^\circ\), the familiar approximately 22° halo.

solution.text:
Atmospheric physics
a.1. Absorbed solar power
Use the intercepting disc and the absorbed fraction: \(P_0=(1-a)\pi R_E^2F_s\).
a.2. Airless temperature
Equate absorbed disc power to emission over 4πRE²: \(T_{g0}=[(1-a)F_s/(4\sigma)]^{1/4}\simeq255\,\mathrm K\), about −18°C.
a.3. One-layer greenhouse temperature
Let PE be ground emission and PA the emission of each atmospheric face. Surface balance gives PE=PA+tswP0. Top-of-atmosphere balance gives tlwPE+PA=P0. Hence \(T_g=[(1+t_{sw})/(1+t_{lw})]^{1/4}T_{g0}\simeq286\,\mathrm K\), about 13°C.
b.1. Diatomic vibrational frequency
The relative coordinate has reduced mass μ=mAmB/(mA+mB). Thus \(\omega_d=\sqrt{k(m_A+m_B)/(m_Am_B)}\).
b.2. Vibrational photon
Harmonic-oscillator adjacent levels differ by \(E_p=\hbar\omega_d\).
b.3. Doppler-shift convention
For fixed incoming lab frequency fin, the molecule sees f′≈fin(1+v/c). Thus if fin=f0 the observed shift is +f0v/c, the convention used in the official solution. If f0 instead denotes the molecule's rest-frame absorption resonance, the resonant laboratory incident frequency is \(f=f_0/(1+v/c)\simeq f_0-f_0v/c\), with shift −f0v/c. The source wording mixes these descriptions. Both yield the same symmetric thermal line profile below, so this signed convention item uses self-review.
b.4. Velocity normalization
The Gaussian integral is √(2πkBT/m), so \(C=\sqrt{m/(2\pi k_BT)}\).
b.5. Thermal spectral profile
Use |v|=c|f−f0|/f0 and the constant Jacobian c/f0. Thus \[p_2(f)\propto\exp\left[-\frac{mc^2(f-f_0)^2}{2k_BT f_0^2}\right].\] If normalized, the prefactor is (c/f0)√[m/(2πkBT)].
b.6. Doppler width and sketch
The curve is a symmetric Gaussian centred at zero, decaying to zero in both tails. The 1/e points are \(f_*-f_0=\pm f_0\sqrt{2k_BT/(mc^2)}\). The field checks the positive half-width.
c.1. Hydrostatic pressure gradient
Balance upward minus downward pressure forces on area A and height dz against weight ρgA dz. This gives \(dp/dz=-\rho g\).
c.2. Ideal-gas gradient
Ideal gas gives ρ=μairp/(RT), hence \(dp/dz=-\mu_{air}gp/(RT)\).
c.3. Isothermal barometric law
Integrate dp/p=−μairg dz/(RT) to obtain \(p(z)=p_0e^{-\mu_{air}gz/(RT)}\).
c.4. Dry adiabatic lapse rate
Adiabatic enthalpy change balances gravitational potential: cp dT+μairg dz=0. Equivalently combine pVγ=constant with hydrostatic equilibrium. Thus \(\Gamma_a=\mu_{air}g/c_p\).
c.5. Buoyancy stability
Parcel and environment temperatures become T−Γaδz and T−Γδz. At equal pressure ρ∝1/T, so net buoyancy acceleration is \[\delta\ddot z=\frac gT(\Gamma-\Gamma_a)\delta z.\] Stability requires Γ<Γa, with \(\omega=\sqrt{g(\mu_{air}g/c_p-\Gamma)/T}\). Equality is neutral, while Γ>Γa gives exponential growth. This sign follows the defined positive lapse rate.
d.1. Clausius-Clapeyron slope
For evaporated mass m, ΔS=Lm/T while ΔV≈(m/μw)RT/ps. Thus \(d p_s/dT=\mu_w Lp_s/(RT^2)\).
d.2. Saturation-pressure law
Integration of dps/ps=(μwL/R)dT/T² gives \[p_s(T)=p_{s0}\exp\left[-\frac{\mu_wL}{R}(1/T-1/T_0)\right].\]
d.3. Cloud formation temperature
The water partial pressure is \(p_w\simeq\phi(\mu_{air}/\mu_w)p\), and dry adiabatic ascent gives p=pi(T/Ti)cp/R. Solve \[\phi\frac{\mu_{air}}{\mu_w}p_i(T_l/T_i)^{7/2}=p_{s0}\exp\left[-\frac{\mu_wL}{R}(1/T_l-1/T_i)\right]\] for the first lower-temperature crossing. With Ti=290.15 K the root is Tl≈286.8 K, or 13.7°C. The total-mass definition of φ changes this only slightly beyond the dilute approximation.
e.1. Prism deviation law
Snell gives internal entry α′=arcsin(sinα/n) and internal exit β′=φ−α′. The external exit angle is β=arcsin(nsinβ′). Therefore \[\delta=\alpha+\arcsin\{n\sin[\varphi-\arcsin(\sin\alpha/n)]\}-\varphi.\] A transmitted ray requires the exit sine magnitude no greater than one.
e.2. Hexagonal-ice deviation plot
The (α,δ) pairs in degrees are approximately (20,27.5),(25,24.6),(30,23.0),(35,22.2),(40,21.8),(45,22.0),(50,22.5),(55,23.4),(60,24.7),(65,26.5),(70,28.7). Draw a smooth curve with a minimum close to α=41°. Label both axes in degrees.
e.3. Bright halo angle
The random crystal orientations concentrate rays near minimum deviation. Symmetric passage gives \(\delta_{min}=2\arcsin[n\sin(\varphi/2)]-\varphi\simeq21.8^\circ\), the familiar approximately 22° halo.
